Browser

|View as Markdown|Agent setup

Give your agent a browser it can return to on later turns. Browser Run keeps the remote browser open, so your agent can continue from the same page with its tabs, cookies, and login session intact while the browser session remains alive.

Use browser tools to interact with websites, inspect pages rendered with JavaScript, or capture screenshots. With internal hostnames, the browser can also open sites that only your agent serves, such as a dev server in its sandbox or a folder in its workspace.

Return to the same browser

A research assistant can open a dashboard, inspect a report, and return to that page on a later turn. The Browser class keeps the remote browser session open between tool calls, including its tabs, cookies, and logins. The browserTool adapters let your harness use that browser through the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP).

The browser runs outside your agent's Durable Object. The object saves its session identifier and reconnects after hibernation, as long as the browser session is still alive. By default, an idle browser stays alive for up to 10 minutes. This does not save a browser permanently: expiry or a crash loses its tabs, cookies, and login state.

Use it with Pi Durable

Start with a Pi Durable agent. Install the Agents SDK alongside the Pi packages:

npm i agents @earendil-works/pi-durable @earendil-works/pi-ai @earendil-works/pi-schema @earendil-works/chord @cloudflare/codemode
yarn add agents @earendil-works/pi-durable @earendil-works/pi-ai @earendil-works/pi-schema @earendil-works/chord @cloudflare/codemode
pnpm add agents @earendil-works/pi-durable @earendil-works/pi-ai @earendil-works/pi-schema @earendil-works/chord @cloudflare/codemode
bun add agents @earendil-works/pi-durable @earendil-works/pi-ai @earendil-works/pi-schema @earendil-works/chord @cloudflare/codemode

The Pi packages are optional peer dependencies of agents, at ~1.6.0. Pi Durable is experimental and its API can change in minor releases, so each agents release supports one Pi minor version. Install the versions your package manager resolves for agents.

This example installs a Browser and PiHarness on a plain Durable Object. Pi chooses when to call the browser tool. Lifecycle starts both components and provides their storage.

The example uses one named assistant for demonstration. In an application, choose an object name for each authenticated user or workspace.

Configure the model, browser, Worker Loader, and Durable Object bindings:

Generate the Env type with wrangler types. The LOADER binding runs the model's browser code in a new Dynamic Worker for each call, with no network access. The code reaches the browser only through the browser API.

browserTool does not use Code Mode, but keep @cloudflare/codemode installed. agents/browser still exports the legacy browser tools, which need it.

To try persistence, send two prompts to the same assistant within the browser's idle timeout:

The second turn can use the existing tab. Pi stores a returned screenshot as an image in the tool result. An image-capable model can see it, and a UI can display it from the transcript. This example's HTTP response only returns the final text; refer to Watch sessions from clients to build a UI.

Tabs, logins, and interruptions

Each Pi conversation gets its own active tab by default. Sessions, forks, and subagents can work on different pages, but cookies and logins remain shared within the Browser. A tab scope is not a separate browser profile. Use separate browsers when users need separate login sessions.

Within a conversation, browser calls run sequentially, and wait for any of your own sessions in the same scope opened with lock: true. The wait does not count toward timeoutMs. The model can use sessionId: "active" in its CDP commands to return to its active tab. To share a tab deliberately, pass the same scope string to the Pi tools.

If a browser expires, closes, or crashes, the next use creates a replacement. The result's notice tells a returning scope that its previous browser state is gone. The tool runs against the new browser. It does not restore the old session. notice also tells the model when the page opened new tabs, or when another conversation closed its tab or is working in it too.

Pi does not automatically replay a browser call interrupted by eviction: repeating it could submit a form or click a button twice. The model receives an interrupted result and can decide how to continue. Each call times out after timeoutMs, which defaults to 60 seconds.

When the harness aborts a browser call, for example because the user stopped the conversation, a call still waiting for its tab gives up, and a running call ends with an error result and frees the tab. Anything its code already did in the browser stays done. This applies to the Pi, AI SDK, and TanStack AI adapters.

Set keepAliveMs, recording, and hostname guardrails on browserRun(binding, options). From your application, call browser.liveView() to let a person inspect or control the same browser, and browser.close() to close it. The persistent browser currently supports Browser Run's Chromium engine.

Use it in Pi's code mode

Pi Durable's code mode lets the model write one script that calls several tools. Install Pi's code mode extension beside the browser tool, and scripts can call tools.browser({ code }) with no other setup. Code mode needs @earendil-works/pi-codemode and a CodemodeSandboxDurableObject deployed as its own Worker. For setup, refer to the Pi Code Mode README ↗︎.

  • tools.browser() resolves to the run as an object, { status, executionId, result, error, logs, notice }, including when the browser code fails, so check status.
  • A screenshot's result is an image block. Pass it to image() so the model sees it.
  • A script's browser calls run in its conversation's tab, one at a time, even under Promise.all.
  • The browser code is still a string inside the script, and each call runs in its own Dynamic Worker, as a direct call does.

Use another harness

Internal hostnames are a capability of the browser, independent of your agent harness. The Agents SDK provides browser-tool adapters for Pi Durable, AI SDK, and TanStack AI. To connect another harness, implement a tool with browser.session(). No prebuilt adapter is required.

Harness Import Usage
Pi Durable browserTool from agents/browser/pi Install in a Pi registry extension's tools array.
AI SDK browserTool from agents/browser/ai-sdk Add to the tools object passed to generateText or streamText.
TanStack AI browserTool from agents/browser/tanstack-ai Add to the tools array passed to chat.
Other harnesses Browser from agents/browser Implement a tool using browser.session(); no prebuilt adapter is required.

For example, create an AI SDK tool inside your Durable Object:

Unlike Pi, the AI SDK and TanStack AI adapters share one active tab when scope is omitted. Pass your conversation identifier to give each conversation its own active tab. The AI SDK adapter exposes screenshots to your UI and sends the model a text summary. TanStack AI omits screenshots and directs the model to read page content instead.

For a harness without a prebuilt adapter, or to drive the browser from your own code, call browser.session({ scope }). This works whether you use an existing framework or write your own harness. It returns the connection that browserTool is built on, with the same sessionId: "active" handling. Close it when you are done to save the scope's active tab and get a report of what happened to the browser:

report.notices holds the same report as sentences for the model, the ones browserTool returns in its notice.

To give model-written code the same browser object that browserTool does, for example in a sandbox of your own, pass it session.functions, the browser.* functions bound to the session. Describe them to the model with this.browser.functionDocs(), which returns { functions, rules }: the functions in Markdown, and the rules for using them. Add rules about how your own code runs, such as its timeouts and what happens to screenshots.

Runs in one scope drive one tab. If your runs can overlap with each other or with browserTool calls, open the session with lock: true. It takes the scope's lock at its first call and holds it until close(). Other locking sessions in the scope, including browserTool runs, wait for it in order instead of failing. To wait for the lock before your own time limit starts, call await session.lock({ signal }) first. session.waitedForLockMs reports how long the session waited.

Caution

A locking session holds the lock until close(), even if its signal aborts, it loses the browser, or you stop using it. Until then, other locking sessions in the scope wait until the Durable Object restarts. Close every locking session in a finally block, including when connecting failed.

To share a tab with a Pi conversation, use conversationScope(String(conversationId)) from agents/browser. It returns the scope that the Pi browserTool uses for that conversation. It takes a string and throws on an empty one.

Internal hostnames

Agents that build websites need to check their work in a real browser. Internal hostnames let your agent's browser preview a dev server running in a container without exposing that server to the public Internet.

Internal hostnames give the browser sites that your agent serves instead of the Internet, such as static assets in an R2 bucket, a folder in the agent's workspace, a dev server in its sandbox, or another Worker. Only this browser can reach these hostnames.

Requests for an internal hostname do not leave Cloudflare. Browser Run sends them to your Worker through outbound Workers, and the Browser runs the matching host's fetch function inside your Durable Object, so it can use the object's bindings and state.

Add internal hostnames

To add internal hostnames, make sure you have Agents SDK v0.31.0 ↗︎ or later installed. Pass internalHosts to browserRun(). This configuration works with the browser-tool adapters or a tool you implement using browser.session():

Each host has either a fetch function or a worker, and an optional description that the model reads:

  • A host with fetch runs that function in your Durable Object for each request and returns its Response.
  • A host with worker, a service binding or a ctx.exports entrypoint, sends requests straight to that Worker, without passing through your Durable Object.

fetch hosts need two pieces of wiring. Export InternalHostRouter from your Worker's main module and pass it as router. Browser Run calls it, and it calls your Durable Object's fetchInternalHost() method. The Agent class has this method built in, so leave it out on an Agent. If you have more than one Browser on a Durable Object, use message.browser to pick the one it names.

browserTool lists each host, with its description, in the tool's description. The model can open http://assets.internal/ or call browser.listHosts() to see each host and what it points at.

Let the model choose what a host serves

A host with only fetch always serves the same thing. Add a target schema and the model chooses what the host serves. In its browser code, the model calls browser.assignHost(), and then navigates to the URL it returns:

The target is checked against the schema, stored, and passed to your fetch function as its second argument. target accepts a Standard JSON Schema ↗︎, such as Zod 4.2 or later, ArkType, or Valibot through its adapter, which also types the argument. It also accepts a plain JSON Schema object, which leaves the argument typed as unknown.

The model picks the target. If part of it becomes a path, URL, or command in your fetch function, restrict it in the schema, for example with an enum, a pattern, or a range, as site.internal does with its folder.

Assignments last until they are cleared. They survive the browser being replaced, Durable Object eviction, and redeploys. An assignable host responds with a 502 until it has a target. The model can call browser.clearHost({ host }) to remove one. From your own code, use this.browser.internalHosts.assign(host, target), .clear(host), and .list().

Limits

  • A browser can have at most eight internal hostnames.
  • Hostnames are bare, lowercase names ending in .internal, .test, .example, or .invalid, such as preview.internal, not http://preview.internal:5173. These suffixes never resolve on the public Internet, so a host cannot shadow a real site.
  • Internal hosts use plain HTTP on port 80. They do not support HTTPS or WebSockets, so a dev server's hot reload cannot connect.
  • The set of hostnames is fixed when the browser starts. Changing the set replaces the browser on its next use. Changing a fetch function does not. Pointing a worker host at a different Worker does not either, so call browser.close() after that change.
  • Guardrails do not apply to internal hosts. Set allowedDomains: [] to let the browser reach only its internal hosts.
  • When a host's fetch function throws, the browser receives a 502 and the error is logged. The page does not see the error message.
  • Internal hosts only work when your Worker is deployed. In local development, the browser starts without them and logs a warning.
  • Install the Browser on a top-level Durable Object or Agent. Sub-agents are not supported yet.

Caution

Any page open in the browser over plain HTTP can send requests to internal hosts, including a page on another internal host. Chrome blocks these requests from HTTPS pages as mixed content. Set allowedDomains: [] unless the model needs the public Internet. If requests to a host have side effects, check that their Origin header names that host.

Live View and human takeover

Live View lets a person watch or control a running browser in real time. Use it when a step needs a human, such as a login, multi-factor authentication (MFA), a CAPTCHA, or sensitive input.

Hand off to a person

Call browser.liveView() from your application to get links into the same browser the model uses. It lists every open tab in the Browser, across all scopes. It does not start a browser: it returns undefined when no browser is open, or when the browser has closed or expired.

For example, add a method to the Durable Object that returns the browser's web pages and their Live View links. Call it from your Worker after you authenticate the user:

browser.liveView() returns an object with the following fields:

Field Description
sessionId The Browser Run session ID.
targets One entry per open tab, with its targetId, its Live View url, and the tab's current pageUrl, title, and type.
expiresInMs How long the Live View URLs remain valid for starting a connection, about five minutes.

Pass mode: "tab" for an interactive page view, or mode: "devtools" for the full DevTools inspector. Omit mode to use the default view from Browser Run.

browserTool does not pause a run while a person acts. Hand off between turns instead:

  1. The model reaches a step it cannot complete, such as a login page, and asks the user for help.
  2. Your application calls browser.liveView() and shows the link to the user.
  3. The user completes the step in Live View.
  4. On the next turn, the model continues in the same browser, with the new cookies and login in place.

If the person closes the model's active tab, the model's next result says that the tab was closed.

Caution

Live View URLs are bearer credentials. Anyone with a link can control the browser, including the sites it is logged in to. Show the links only to trusted, authenticated users. Do not give them to the model, and do not store them. Call browser.liveView() again to create fresh links.

Close the browser

Call browser.close() to end the browser. It deletes the Browser Run session and returns false if no browser was open. The next use of the Browser starts a new browser, and the result's notice tells each scope that worked in the old browser that its state is gone.

Recording

Session recording captures a Browser Run session as structured rrweb events: DOM changes, input, and navigation, not video. Use recordings to audit or debug what an agent did in its browser.

To turn on recording, set recording: true in the provider options:

The option applies to every browser the Browser creates, including replacements after a restart. Each Browser Run session has its own recording. A recording is finalized when its session closes, after browser.close() or when the browser is idle for longer than keepAliveMs.

Note the Browser Run session ID while the browser is open, then fetch the recording after the browser closes:

getBrowserRecording() uses the Browser Run REST API, so it needs your account ID and an API token with access to Browser Run. The Workers binding cannot read recordings. Recordings are retained for 30 days and capped at two hours per session.

Caution

A persistent browser's recording spans every turn and every scope that shares the Browser, until that browser closes. If several users share one Browser, one recording can include all of their activity. rrweb masks input fields by default, but treat every recording as sensitive.

Browser API

The model writes an async arrow function against a browser object. Methods with arguments take a single object:

Method Description
browser.cdp({ method, params?, sessionId?, timeoutMs? }) Send a CDP command and return its result.
browser.attachToTarget({ targetId, timeoutMs? }) Attach to a tab, make it active, and return { sessionId } for page-scoped calls.
browser.spec({ domain? }) List the CDP protocol's domains, or return one domain's commands, events, and types.
browser.getDebugLog({ limit? }) Return recent CDP traffic for this call, including sends, receives, and warnings.
browser.clearDebugLog() Clear the debug log.
browser.listHosts() List the internal hostnames and what each one points at.
browser.assignHost({ host, target }) Point an assignable internal host at a target and return { url }.
browser.clearHost({ host }) Remove an internal host's target.

listHosts() is available when the browser has internal hostnames, and assignHost() and clearHost() when one of them has a target schema. The tool's description covers this API and the CDP mistakes models commonly make, so the model does not need a discovery pass first.

The browser API also follows these rules:

  • sessionId: "active" addresses the scope's active tab. Browser.* and Target.* commands take no sessionId.
  • A sessionId from browser.attachToTarget() keeps working in later calls.
  • Each call runs in a new Dynamic Worker with no network access. fetch() and connect() are blocked, so browser is the code's only way out.
  • Each call times out after timeoutMs, which defaults to 60 seconds.
  • Results are cut to about 24,000 characters, and console output to 100 lines. A screenshot can be at most 1 MB. To capture a long page, take a viewport screenshot or use JPEG.

The model cannot send these commands, because your application owns the browser and its Live View links:

  • Browser.close, Browser.crash, and Browser.crashGpuProcess. To close a tab, the model sends Target.closeTarget.
  • Cloudflare.getLiveView and Cloudflare.handoff.
  • Target.sendMessageToTarget and Target.exposeDevToolsProtocol, which could otherwise send the other refused commands.

Read pages without a browser

To read a page or document at a known URL, use the web_fetch tool instead of a browser. It does not start a browser, so each read is a single HTTP request. It also converts PDFs and Office documents to Markdown and splits long pages into parts the model can read in turn.

Use browserTool when the page needs a browser:

  • The page renders its content with JavaScript.
  • The page needs a login, or the model must click, type, or move through several pages.
  • The agent must return to the same page, tabs, or session on a later turn.
  • You need a screenshot of the page.

Legacy browser tools

createBrowserTools and createBrowserRuntime from agents/browser/ai are deprecated. They keep working until they are removed, but will not change. The same applies to createBrowserTools from agents/browser/tanstack-ai, to BrowserConnector from agents/browser, to the Quick Action tools, and to the Think browser tools in @cloudflare/think/tools/browser, which are built on them. New code should use Browser with browserTool.

You might still use the legacy tools for the following:

  • Your own browser. Connect to a CDP endpoint you manage with cdpUrl. Browser supports only Browser Run's Chromium engine.
  • Kitesurf. A Kitesurf browser lives only as long as its CDP WebSocket, so it cannot be a persistent browser.
  • Approval or human handoff within a run. The durable Code Mode runtime can pause a run for approval and resume it with the browser session intact. browserTool does not pause runs.

You do not need the legacy tools to get a fresh browser for each run. With browserTool, call browser.close() after a turn, or set a short keepAliveMs, so the next run starts a new browser. To read a page without a browser, use the web_fetch tool.

Basic pattern

Create browser tools with the Browser Run and Worker Loader bindings, then pass those tools to your model call. The model writes code against a cdp object in the browser_execute tool, described in Legacy CDP methods.

Browser tools must be created from inside a Durable Object, such as an Agent. The durable runtime facet and the session store live on its ctx. The helper exposes one durable CDP tool plus stateless Quick Action tools when a browser binding is present:

Tool Description
browser_execute Run sandboxed code against a live browser over CDP — screenshots, DOM reads, JavaScript evaluation, and more.
browser_markdown Read a page or raw HTML as Markdown.
browser_extract Extract structured data from a page with AI.
browser_links List links on a page.
browser_scrape Scrape specific elements by CSS selector.

The TanStack AI createBrowserTools returns only browser_execute. To discover protocol surface, the model calls cdp.spec() or the runtime's built-in codemode.search() and codemode.describe().

Configuration

The legacy tools use the same BROWSER and LOADER bindings as browserTool. Refer to Use it with Pi Durable for the Wrangler configuration. Unlike browserTool, they also need a CodemodeRuntime export from your Worker:

The @cloudflare/codemode/vite plugin adds the CodemodeRuntime export automatically.

createBrowserTools and createBrowserRuntime accept the following options:

Option Default Description
browser — Browser Run binding.
cdpHeaders — Headers for CDP URL discovery, such as Cloudflare Access headers.
cdpUrl — A custom CDP endpoint. Takes priority over browser when both are set.
ctx The current Agent's state The Durable Object that hosts the runtime facet and session store.
loader Required Worker Loader binding for sandboxed execution.
name "browser" Runtime name, the durable identity of executions.
quickActions On with a browser binding Quick Action tools to include. Pass false or { actions, maxChars, options }.
session { mode: "one-shot" } Session lifecycle mode, recording, and engine.
store Durable Object storage Durable store for Browser Run session IDs.
timeout 30000 Execution timeout in milliseconds, also used as the per-command CDP timeout.

Provide either browser or cdpUrl. When only cdpUrl is set, the Quick Action tools are skipped.

Session lifecycle

By default, each execution gets a fresh browser session, torn down when the run ends (one-shot). Pass a session option for two more modes:

  • one-shot (default) — fresh session per execution; deterministic cleanup when the execution reaches a terminal status.
  • reuse — a named shared session that persists across executions until explicitly closed or swept.
  • dynamic — starts one-shot; the model can promote the session with cdp.startSession() (for example, after logging in to a page) so later executions continue in the same browser.

Sessions are tracked durably in the Durable Object's storage, so they survive hibernation and approval pauses. A run that pauses for human approval resumes with its browser session, tabs, and cookies intact. If Browser Run expires the session while a pause waits, the resume surfaces a clear error and the model starts over.

Host-side helpers

For host-side wiring, use createBrowserRuntime, which returns { runtime, connector, tools }:

Call connector.sweep() from a scheduled task. connector.liveView() returns the shared session's tabs and Live View URLs, with each tab's current pageUrl, so an agent UI can label tabs and skip blank or internal pages.

Approval and human handoff

With createBrowserRuntime, the Code Mode runtime can pause a run with the browser session intact. A handoff follows this pattern:

  1. The model calls cdp.getLiveViewUrl() to get a link to the current tab.
  2. The agent surfaces the link to the user.
  3. The model makes an approval-gated call, so the run pauses durably.
  4. After approval, the run resumes against the same session.

Pass mode: "tab" for an interactive page view, or mode: "devtools" for the full DevTools inspector. The URL is valid for about five minutes. Call cdp.getLiveViewUrl() again to create a fresh URL.

Every cdp.* call is recorded in the runtime's durable log. If a run pauses for approval or the sandbox aborts, resuming replays the log and continues. Connector calls must therefore be sequential and deterministic. Model code must not use Promise.all for CDP calls, and the tool instructions enforce this. The sessionId from cdp.attachToTarget() is a stable handle that stays valid across pause and resume.

Legacy CDP methods

Model code in browser_execute uses a cdp object. Methods with arguments take a single object:

Method Description
cdp.send({ method, params?, sessionId?, timeoutMs? }) Send a CDP command and return its result.
cdp.attachToTarget({ targetId, timeoutMs? }) Attach to a tab and return { sessionId }, a handle for page-scoped send calls.
cdp.spec() Return the searchable, normalized CDP protocol description from the live browser.
cdp.getDebugLog({ limit? }) Return recent CDP traffic, including sends, receives, and warnings, for this run.
cdp.clearDebugLog() Clear the debug log.

browser_execute also provides these methods:

Method Availability Description
cdp.getLiveViewUrl({ targetId?, mode? }) Chromium sessions Create a Live View URL for a tab.
cdp.startSession() reuse, dynamic Promote or ensure the shared session and return its info.
cdp.sessionInfo() reuse, dynamic Return the shared session info, or null.
cdp.closeSession() reuse, dynamic Close the shared session.
cdp.resetSession() reuse, dynamic Close and replace the shared session.

Session recording

To record legacy sessions, set recording: true in the session option:

A recording is finalized after the session closes. Capture the session ID with connector.sessionInfo() while the session is alive, then fetch the recording with getBrowserRecording(), as described in Recording. A recording on a shared reuse or dynamic session spans the full session lifetime, including every user that shares the session key.

Kitesurf

To use Kitesurf with browser_execute, select it in the session options:

A Kitesurf browser is scoped to its CDP WebSocket, so it supports only one-shot execution. Session reuse, pause and resume, Live View, recording, keepAliveMs, protocol discovery with cdp.spec(), and Kitesurf-backed Quick Actions are not available.

Quick Action tools

createQuickActionTools from agents/browser/ai gives the model tools for Browser Run Quick Actions. Each call is a one-shot request: Browser Run loads the page in a new browser, returns the result, and closes the browser. Quick Actions need only the browser binding, so they do not need a Durable Object, Worker Loader, or sandbox. To read a page, prefer the web_fetch tool.

Quick Actions do not share a browser or a login with browserTool. A site the model logged in to with browserTool is not logged in for a Quick Action. To read a protected page, pass credentials such as cookies or authenticate through options.

Pass actions to choose the tools, maxChars to bound results, and options for request settings:

Every Quick Action result is bounded to maxChars, which defaults to 50,000 characters, to protect the model context window while preserving the result shape. Host-supplied request options, such as cookies, authenticate, gotoOptions, and viewport, are passed once through options and are not exposed to the model.

Quick Actions require a Worker compatibility_date of 2026-03-24 or later and remote: true on the browser binding for local wrangler dev.
